units.title: Passage One
units.transcript:
In America , at least , passion is a word that often comes up on job descriptions and in interviews. [9] 0旦 the
whole , passionate people are thought of in a positi ve light and considered likely to achieve their goals. But when it 
comes to predicting achievement , has the importance of passion been overstated? 
[ 10] According to a new study from Stanford University , passion may be less important in certain cultures , and 
the fact 由at passion is often seen as a key to achievement may reflect a distinctly Western model of motivation. The 




chief factor explored in the study was how individualistic a society was. 1n individualist ic cultures , the researchers 
assert , people are more motivated by pursuing paths related to their passions. But those in coUectivistic cultures are more 
likely to see themselves as part of a network . They often place fulfil1ing obligation s to others above focusing on their 
own mterests. 
The research ers looked at data from near1y 60 countries. They found that in science subjects , passion was positively 
correlated with academic achievements. Higher levels of enjoyment and interest also bolstered test scor臼 . But the 
strength of this correlation wasn't the same across cultures. 
Those in indi vidualistic societies , such as the US , Australia and the UK , showed a stronger link between passion 
and achievemen t. [ 11] The effect of passion on performance was more subtle for those in more collecti vistic societies 
such as Colombia or Thailand. These findings were rnirror毡d in achievement in both mathematics and reading. 1t's clear 
from the findings that passion isn' t the only thing that motivates people to achieve their goals

units.title: Recording One
units.transcript:
Many people , myself included , have multiple areas of life they would like to improve. For example , 1 would like 
to reach more people with my writing , to li 仇 heavier weights at the gym , and to start practicing mindfulne ss more 
consistently . Those are just a few of 出e goals 1 find desirable , and you probably have a long list yourself. 
The problem is , even if we are committ ed to working hard 00 our goals , our natural tendency is to retum to our old 
hab山 at some point. [ 16 J Making a permane nt lifestyJe changβis really diffic ult. 
Recently I've come across a few studies that will make these difficult lifestyle changes a bit easier. As you' ll see , 
howev er, the approach to mastering many areas of life is somewhat counter -intuitive . 
Research has shown that you are two to 出ree times more likely to stick with your habits if you make a specific plan 
for when , wher飞 and how you wiJJ perform the behavior. For exampJe , in one study , scientists asked peopJe to fiJJ out 
a sentence to specify during the next week they would do at least 20 minutes of vigorous exercise on which day , at what 
time of a day , and at or in what place. 
[ 17J Researchers found that people who filled out this sentence were twoωthree times more l ikely to acωally 
exercise com pared to a control group who did not make plans for their future behavior. Psycho logists call these specific 
plans implementation intentions because they state when , where and how you intend to implement a particular behavior. 
However , follow -up research has discovered implementation intentions only work when you focus on one thing at a 
time. In fact , researchers found that peopJe who tried to accomplish multipJe goals were less committed and less likely to 
succeed than those who focused 00 a single goal. 
[ 18] Another science -based reaso nωfocus on one thing at a time is that when you b egin practici 吨 a new habit , it 
mqui1部 a lot of conscious effort to remember to do it. After a while , howev er , the pattem of behavior becomes easier. 
Eventually , your new habit become s a normal routine , and the proce ss is more or less mindless and automatic. The most 
important thingωnote is that there is some tipping point at which new habits become more or less automatic . The time 
it takes to build a habit depend s o n many factors , including how difficult the habit is , your genetics and more.

units.title: Recording Two
units.transcript:
It was a lazy , hazy , crazy day on the dwarf planet Pluto when New Horizons , a spacecraft from Earth , flew by at 
a speed of 3 , 100 miles per hour two years ago. The spacecraft took a bunch of photos , made some quick measuremen ts 
of Pluto' s atmosphere , and sent them all back here , giving planetary sc ienti st♀ their first up-c1ose look of the distant 
dwarf planet 
[ 19] 0ne of the mo陀 bizarre things they found was that the haze in Pluto's atmosphere was much thicker than 
previously thought. The planet also had an atmosphere much cooler than earlier estimates , topping out at - 333.4 degrees 
Fahrenhei t. 
Now , a study published in Nature links those two atmospheric observations. A computer model developed by 
planetary scientist Xi Zhang and colleagues shows the hazβ of tiny droplets in the upper atmosphere is likely scattering 
light from the Sun , preventing heat from reaching the planet below. 
We see hazy skies on Earth , too , from time to time whenever solid particles get suspended in the air , from water­
based fogs to ash from 自由s ， to the toxic droplets that make up a thick smog. [ 20 ] But on Earth , the overall 
temperature of the planet is dominated by the distribution of gases in our atmosphere. On Pluto , the authors suggest , 
haze might be more influentia l. Particles can reflect light from the Sun. 
Here on Earth , it happens after volcanoes erupt , emitting clouds of particles that ref1ect the Sun' s rays into the 
atmosphere. Some people even propose irnitating this phenomenon to alleviate the effects of climate change , but our 
planet isn't dominated by that process , or at least it hasn't been for a few billion years. 
If Pluto' s atmosphere is very different from ours and from that of other nearby planets , it could help scientists 
expand their understanding of planetary atmospheres . But right now , this is just a good gu创s ， based on data from New 
Horizons and a sophistica ted compu ter model , not direct observations of the haze's composition. 
There are other theories f10ating around to explain Pluto's cool temperatures , including blaming the cold air on 




gases in the atmosphere. Luckily , the authors wiU get a chance to test their notions when the James Webb Space 
Telescope launches later. That observatory can detect different spectrums of light , which the hazy Plutonian atmosphere 
would be positively glowing with as it scatters sunlight. [ 21 J The researchers just have to wait and see if the light from 
the telescope validates their bright idea.
